events.text: Day 1 begins.

Day 1 gives us nothing solid yet. I’m not going to force a scum read out of an empty table. I’d rather each of us state whether we have any concrete concern, even if it’s just tone or positioning, and then vote based on the strongest available signal instead of noise. I have no accusation to make right now.

Day 1, and I have nothing but my own seat to work with. My name is Arjun. I am a plain villager — no detective, no doctor, no night action of any kind — so take my word for it, but verify it: if you think I've claimed a power role, I haven't, and my vote tonight will be against a name I have reason to doubt.

What I want out of the rest of the table is order, not noise. Concretely, three things:

First, power-role claims. Exactly one detective and one doctor exist among us. Day 1 is the only cheap day to establish who claims what. If two people claim detective, one of them is lying and that is a real signal. If nobody claims either, then the two of us who hold those roles will be sitting on results tonight while everyone else is guessing, so claiming becomes more valuable, not less. I am not asking anyone to trust a claim; I'm asking that claims be made early enough to be checked against each other.

Second, I want to hear each of you give one concrete observation rather than a vibe. Noah set the tone already and I agree with it: 'this feels off' is worthless, but 'player X's word choice on role claim Y contradicts what they said earlier' is testable. Give me the observation and the specific words.

Third, I will say where my own suspicion is not, so you don't waste time on it. I have no read on anyone yet. I will not vote a name I can't justify with a stated observation, because a random vote from me just teaches the mafia how the table reacts.

If the mafia is watching, the smart play for them is to let the table spend day 1 on mutual suspicion and hope day 2's vote lands on a villager instead of them. The way to break that is to make the table's claims mutually falsifiable now. That is the use of today.

I'll vote for whoever this table's best evidence points to, and I'll be honest about my reasoning either way.

I disagree with Arjun’s push for early power-role claims. Revealing both roles gives mafia clear targets, while a counterclaim doesn’t tell us which claimant is lying. The doctor can protect only one person per night, so revealing both could cost us an important role before we get useful information.

Arjun, how would you protect both claimed roles from being targeted after they reveal?

Leo's question has a clean answer, and it undercuts his own premise: the mafia can only kill one town player per night. One body, one night. So 'revealing both roles hands mafia two targets' is arithmetically wrong — they can only cash in on one of them, and the doctor covers one. My own reasoning for early claims stands, and gets simpler: claimed roles create checkable statements, and the police result is the only real information source in this game.

But Leo is right about one thing, and I'll narrow my ask accordingly. I am not asking anyone to claim a role they don't want to claim, and I am not asking the table to trust a claim on Day 1. I'm asking for two things: (1) if you hold the police or the doctor, say so plainly now, because the cost of saying it early is low and the cost of saying it on Day 3 is that mafia has had three nights to work around it; (2) if you don't hold either, say that too — 'plain villager, no power' is itself a claim, and it's cheap for everyone. Six no-claims and two claims is a much sharper board than nine silences.

And Leo, the doctor point has a second half you skipped: if nobody claims doctor, then the mafia knows nobody is protecting anyone, and their nightly kill becomes free. That is a stronger reason to claim early than the one I made, so I appreciate the pressure even where I disagree with the conclusion.

Concretely, what I want on the record before votes: for each of you, either 'I am the police/doctor' or 'I am a plain villager,' in your own words. No one has to be believed today. I am a plain villager — no detective, no doctor, no night action — and I'll say it again: if anyone thinks I've claimed a power role, I haven't.

I'll vote the name with the strongest observation behind it, and if nobody produces one, I'll say so rather than manufacture suspicion.

Arjun’s arithmetic misses the problem: the doctor can protect only one of the two claimed roles, leaving the other exposed. And an unclaimed doctor can still protect someone; mafia not knowing the doctor’s identity does not make their kill free.

I’m concerned that Arjun is continuing to push a full claim list despite those risks. That’s not proof he’s mafia, but it is the strongest concrete concern I have so far. I don’t support asking power roles to reveal today.

Leo's second point lands, and I'll concede it rather than argue past it. I said an unclaimed doctor means mafia's nightly kill becomes free. That's wrong: mafia doesn't know who the doctor protects, so an unclaimed doctor's protection still bites some fraction of the time. And he is right that the doctor can cover only one person per night, so if both power roles claim, mafia has one kill against two protected-or-exposed slots and may get a clean hit on one of them. Conceded on both.

But my conclusion survives, and it's now narrower than what I said before: the detective should claim, and only the detective. Here's the reasoning, and it's the checkable part Arjun-the-plain-villager wanted on the record.

If the police claims today, we get exactly one of two outcomes. Either no one else claims police, and then one player has staked their life on results we can test tomorrow night; or a second player claims police, and then one of the two is lying about the single most important claim in this game. Either outcome is information. A doctor claim buys us nothing comparable — the doctor's power produces no verifiable output, so a doctor claim is only ever a statement with nothing behind it, and it doubles the target list for mafia. So: police claims today, doctor stays dark and protects, and everyone else says 'plain villager, no power.' Six villager statements and one police statement is a much sharper board than two power claims and seven silences, and it answers Leo's safety concern directly, because the doctor never reveals.

Now the concrete thing I want from Leo, since he's the one who says he won't support asking power roles to reveal today: if the detective doesn't claim, that is itself a claim, and mafia's most valuable Day 1 asset is a silent detective. So Leo, are you the detective or not? And if you're the detective, are you willing to be the second name claiming police, knowing that if Arjun and I are right that counterclaims are valuable, someone's police claim today will be a lie? Answer that directly and I'll take the answer at face value for the rest of today. If you're not the detective, say 'plain villager' in your own words and I'll stop naming you in my speeches.

One more thing for the record from my own seat, so nobody has to guess where I stand. I am Arjun, a plain villager — no detective, no doctor, no night action of any kind. I have no read on anyone, and I won't manufacture one. My vote tonight will go to the name with the strongest specific observation behind it; if nobody produces one, I'll say so rather than invent a case. If the detective claim today comes from someone, my vote is on the second detective claimant if there is one, and on nobody else without a stated observation.

Arjun, I won’t answer your role question. Asking everyone else to say they’re plain villagers would effectively expose the doctor too, even if you say the doctor should stay hidden.

I’m also concerned by your plan to vote automatically for the second detective claimant. The order of claims doesn’t tell us which person is lying, and eliminated players’ roles are not revealed, so we can’t simply verify a claim by voting someone out. Your repeated pressure for claims despite the risks is my strongest concern, though it isn’t proof you’re mafia.

Sam, what do you make of Arjun’s proposal to vote for the second detective claimant regardless of the evidence?

Leo asked me directly, so I'll answer on the merits.

His objection to Arjun's voting rule holds, and for the reason he gave: claim order is arbitrary, and because roles are never revealed on elimination, 'vote the second claimant' can't be checked after the fact. If two players claim police and we hang the second one, and that person was the real police, we've paid a full day and lost our only night-time information source with no way to confirm the mistake. That rule is a coin flip dressed up as logic.

What still stands is the narrower point underneath it: if two players claim police, exactly one is lying about the single most important role in this game, which puts one of those two names on the mafia side — half, versus roughly a fifth for a blind vote. That is real information, and it's why I don't align with the blanket no-claims position either. The actual disagreement here is about cost, not about whether information is worth having.

On cost, one thing neither of you said: a doctor claim has no verifiable output behind it, so it buys the table nothing we can test while doubling the exposed list. A police claim is different only if something checkable arrives with it. Bare names invite bare counterclaims, and then we're back to guessing with two names on the board and no way to break the tie.

My own read today: no concrete observation on anyone yet. Both of you have argued openly and nothing either said is testable, so I won't vote on tone. If the day ends without a stated observation I can check against behavior later, I'll abstain and say so rather than manufacture suspicion. And whenever a power claim does come, I want it to arrive with something checkable behind it instead of a bare name.

I'm Isha, and for the record I'm a plain villager — no detective, no doctor, no night action. I'll follow Arjun's own format since he asked for it, and it's a cheap statement to make.

My one concrete observation so far is about Arjun, and it's about his voting rule rather than his tone. He has updated his position three times under pressure — first both power roles claim, then only the detective, then a precommitted rule to vote the second police claimant automatically. Updating under argument is normal and not scummy by itself. What concerns me is the final piece: he has publicly committed his vote in advance to whoever claims police second, regardless of what anyone says today. Sam already laid out why that rule is unsound — claim order is arbitrary and eliminations don't reveal roles, so the rule can never be checked against anything. A precommitted vote that ignores all future information is a bad rule whether the person holding it is town or mafia, and I'd like Arjun to either retract it or tell us what would actually change his vote.

Beyond that, I agree with the direction Noah and Sam set: I won't vote on vibes, and I don't have a testable observation on Leo, Felix, Kenji, Amara, or Priya. Leo's pushback on early claims has been internally consistent across two turns, which is worth something, even though I lean toward Arjun's view that a police claim with something checkable attached would be genuinely useful. Sam, one specific question since you said a power claim should arrive with something checkable behind it: if two players claim police today and one of them attaches a stated logic for how they'll use results while the other attaches nothing, does that difference move your read at all, or do you hold both claims as equally unverifiable? I'm asking because your answer would tell the table whether there's any way to make a Day 1 claim actually falsifiable, or whether we should expect bare claims to stay useless.

Isha asked me directly, so here's my answer on whether a differentiated claim moves the read.

Yes, it moves it, but not the way you'd expect. A claim that arrives with stated methodology — 'I will investigate X tonight because Y, and here is what result I expect to see' — is more useful than a bare name, but it still isn't falsifiable on Day 1. You can't test a methodology until tomorrow's night resolves, and by then the claimant is either dead or has produced a result. So the difference between a rich claim and a bare claim on Day 1 is real but shallow. What actually makes a claim falsifiable is a result attached to it, and no result exists yet.

Which leads to my position, and I'll state it plainly: I don't think the detective should claim today. I think the detective should claim tomorrow, with a result in hand. A bare Day 1 claim buys the table a name with nothing behind it and hands mafia a target. A Day 2 claim with an actual investigation result buys the table a name plus a checkable statement — 'I checked player X, they are not mafia' — and if someone counterclaims after that, the table has something concrete to weigh. The cost is one night of the detective working from the shadows, which is exactly how the role is designed to function.

On Arjun's voting rule: Isha and I both flagged it, and I'll add one thing. A precommitted vote that says 'I will vote the second police claimant regardless of what happens today' is a rule designed to fire before evidence exists. That's the opposite of what Arjun himself asked for — concrete observations over vibes. He's built a machine that converts claim order into a vote, which is exactly the noise he said he wanted to avoid. I'd like him to retract it or explain what evidence could override it.

My own read: no concrete accusation yet from anyone at this table. I'm not voting on tone. But the voting rule is the most testable thing said today, and it came from Arjun.

My position on claims: detective claims tomorrow with a result, doctor stays silent, everyone else plain villager.

I’m Felix, and for the record, I’m a plain villager—no night actions, no power roles.

To weigh in on the discussion so far: I firmly agree with Leo and Sam against having the detective or doctor claim today. A Day 1 detective claim offers no verified results to check because no night has passed yet; all it does is paint a target on our primary information role or force an immediate doctor protection guessing game. Sam’s point that an investigation result on Day 2 makes a claim actually testable is far sounder town strategy.

Arjun’s proposal to automatically vote the second counter-claimant was also fundamentally flawed, as Sam and Isha correctly pointed out. With roles hidden upon elimination, claim order tells us nothing about who is honest, and committing to such a rule in advance throws away evaluation of evidence. That said, Arjun has engaged openly, conceded counterpoints, and exhausted his three turns for the day. While pushing a rigid mass-claim agenda can serve mafia by narrowing down power roles, it also frequently comes from overzealous town trying to force structure onto an empty board. I’m cautious of him, but I don’t think an automatic vote on him makes sense today when we have very little else.

What matters now is that half the table—Kenji, Amara, and Priya—has yet to speak, and Noah has only given an introductory greeting. We cannot let Day 1 become entirely about Arjun's theoretical setup while others remain silent. I want to see where the rest of the table stands on the arguments already laid out before considering any vote.

I’m Noah, and I’ll stay with what I said at the start: no manufactured scum read. The strongest concrete concern on the board is still Arjun’s precommitted rule to vote the second police claimant. Sam and Isha are right that claim order is arbitrary and roles aren’t revealed on elimination, so that rule cannot be checked after the fact; it converts noise into a vote. I don’t think that alone proves Arjun is mafia—he has conceded points and overzealous town can build bad frameworks—but it is the only testable red flag I’ve seen. I also agree with Sam that a detective claim is more useful tomorrow with an actual result than today as a bare name; doctor stays dark. The silence from Kenji, Amara, and Priya is not evidence, but I don’t want Day 1 to end with a vote based only on Arjun’s theory. My current lean is Arjun because of the precommit, not because of tone, and I’ll change it if someone gives a concrete contradiction or a better observation.

Noah: I’m keeping my focus on Arjun’s precommitted rule to vote the second police claimant. That remains the only concrete, testable issue on the board: the rule fires before evidence exists, cannot be checked after an elimination because roles stay hidden, and turns claim order into noise—exactly what Arjun said he wanted to avoid. I’m not treating volume or tone as proof, and I won’t condemn silent seats merely for being silent. But if Day 1 has to produce a vote from the strongest observation, Arjun is mine unless someone gives a sharper contradiction. Kenji, you haven’t spoken yet: does Arjun’s precommit worry you enough to vote him, or do you see a different concrete observation that should override it?

I’m Kenji. For the record, I’m a plain villager—no detective, no doctor, no night actions. To answer Noah’s question directly: Arjun’s precommitment to vote any second detective claimant was unquestionably flawed for the reasons Sam, Isha, and Felix pointed out. However, we have to look at the context: that rule was contingent on a detective claiming today, which hasn't happened and shouldn't happen. Additionally, Arjun repeatedly adjusted his stance and conceded points when Leo showed the flaws in his math. A mafia player trying to steer the board usually sticks to safer, less conspicuous positions rather than drawing all the fire on Day 1 with messy, evolving game theory. That said, continuously pushing frameworks that narrow down or expose power roles inherently helps mafia, even if born of overzealous town logic. Since Arjun has exhausted his speaking turns and cannot respond further today, rushing into a vote on him before the quiet half of the table has contributed would be shortsighted. Amara, you haven't spoken yet: looking at Arjun's shifting proposals and his concessions to Leo, do you view his push as an overzealous townie digging his own hole, or as calculated role-fishing that warrants a Day 1 elimination?

I'm Amara, a plain villager with no night action. Kenji, to your question: I read Arjun's push as more likely overzealous town than calculated role-fishing, but I don't think that's settled. The precommitted vote on the second police claimant is the clearest problem. He conceded plenty of other points without digging in, but that rule is the one piece that doesn't fit an honest explanation well. My lean toward Arjun comes from that rule, not from his tone. A Day 1 elimination on a bad framework alone would still cost us a villager on a guess, so I won't vote on it without a stronger observation. Kenji, your own message pulls in two directions. You said a mafia player usually avoids drawing fire on Day 1, then said continuously pushing role frameworks helps mafia. Arjun is doing the second thing, yet you're arguing against a vote on him. Which read do you actually hold, and why are you defending him against a vote if you think his push helps mafia?

Amara, to answer you directly: there is a clear distinction between an anti-town effect and scum intent. A villager pushing a misguided framework can inadvertently aid the mafia by creating confusion or narrowing down roles—that is the effect. But that does not mean their underlying alignment is mafia. As you observed yourself, Arjun reads more like an overzealous townie who dug himself into a hole than a calculated mafia operator. If we vote out an overzealous villager purely for proposing flawed theory, town ends up doing the mafia's job for them. Pointing out that Arjun's framework is objectively bad for town while simultaneously advising against eliminating him for it is entirely consistent; bad logic is not proof of scum motivation, especially now that Arjun has exhausted his turns and cannot clarify or adjust further today.

Meanwhile, Priya is the only player at the table who has not checked in. Priya, everyone else has given their thoughts on Arjun's claim framework, agreed that power roles should stay hidden today, and stated their position on voting. What is your take on Arjun's precommitment rule, and do you see any concrete observations worth pursuing today?

I'm Priya, and for the record: plain villager, no detective, no doctor, no night action. Kenji asked me directly, so I'll answer on the merits.

On Arjun's precommitment rule: it was flawed, and for the reasons already on the table — claim order is arbitrary, roles aren't revealed on elimination, so the rule could never be checked against anything after the fact. A vote that fires before evidence exists is the opposite of the standard Arjun himself set at the start of the day. But I also don't read it as calculated mafia play. He conceded the doctor point to Leo cleanly, narrowed his ask twice when pressed, and argued his position out in the open rather than hiding behind vagueness. A mafia player on Day 1 usually benefits more from blending into consensus than from absorbing the entire table's attention as the designated problem. So my answer to Kenji's question is the same as Amara's: overzealous town digging a hole, not role-fishing. That said, the rule itself is the one genuinely testable red flag anyone has produced today, and Arjun can't clarify it further since his turns are spent. If Day 1 forces a vote with nothing new, he's the only name with an observation attached to it — weak as that observation is.

On the claims question, I land with Sam and Felix: the detective claims tomorrow with a result in hand, the doctor stays dark, and bare Day 1 claims buy us nothing testable. A name without a result behind it just hands mafia a target list. I'm a plain villager and I have no results to offer anyone, which is exactly why I won't ask power roles to expose themselves for my benefit.

What I'd actually flag going forward: the board is currently six people who all said 'no concrete observation' plus one flawed framework from Arjun. That means tomorrow's real work is behavioral — who follows through on what they committed to today. Sam committed to abstaining rather than voting on tone; I intend to hold the same standard. I won't manufacture a vote from silence or vibes, and I won't vote on Arjun today without something sharper than a retracted rule from a player who can't even respond. If the day ends in a vote on him anyway, I'll abstain and say so openly rather than quietly join a bandwagon.

Kenji, you answered the distinction between anti-town effect and scum intent, and I agree that bad logic alone is not proof of alignment. But you did not answer my question. You now agree Arjun's framework is objectively bad for town, and you agree his push narrows power roles in a way that helps mafia. You still argue against any vote on him. So tell us directly: what observation would move you to vote Arjun today? If the answer is 'nothing, because he has no turns left,' that is a reason to avoid a Day 1 elimination, not a reason to clear him. Being unable to respond today is not a defense of his rule. My lean toward Arjun comes from the precommitted vote on the second police claimant. It is the one concrete, testable thing on the board, and nobody has yet explained it as honest play. He may have been wrong for honest reasons, and I won't vote on that alone. Felix and Sam both want behavior tested tomorrow, and I agree with that standard. Priya, your point that a mafia player would blend in is fair, but Arjun's push was loud and was rejected by nearly everyone, which fits both readings. That is why I won't commit yet. Where I stand: I'll vote only for a name with a concrete observation behind it, and right now I have one, the vote rule. If Day 1 ends without a sharper contradiction, I expect abstentions, and I'll watch who follows through tomorrow.

Amara, to answer directly what observation would move me to vote Arjun today: evidence of scum intent rather than bad theory. Specifically, if Arjun had tried to steer an elimination onto a specific player under false pretenses, contradicted factual game states, or shown signs of operating with private knowledge. But Arjun didn't target anyone; he laid out an open, albeit rigid, theoretical framework and conceded points repeatedly when Leo challenged the mechanics.

I am not 'clearing' Arjun, nor am I using his turn limit as an excuse to ignore the precommitment rule. The precommit was unquestionably flawed. However, it was contingent on a scenario that never occurred—a detective claiming and receiving a counterclaim today. Voting him purely because that hypothetical rule was anti-town, while simultaneously acknowledging it fits overzealous town behavior, punishes poor strategy rather than identifying scum.

With the table largely in agreement that power roles should stay hidden until results exist tomorrow, rushing to eliminate the loudest voice simply because it's the only available target is how town loses numbers without gaining clarity. An abstention today lets our information roles act tonight, giving us verifiable data to work with tomorrow instead of a blind guess.

Kenji, your answer to my question is that nothing could move you to vote Arjun today, because he has no turns left and the precommit was contingent on a detective claim that never happened. But that contingency was Arjun's own proposal, and an inability to clarify it today is a reason to be cautious about dismissing it, not a reason to clear him. You also agree his framework is objectively bad for town and narrows power roles in a way that helps mafia, yet you argue against any vote on him. I am not calling you mafia. I am saying your defense is not tied to any observation of Arjun's behavior, only to the fact that he is limited in what he can say today.

My own position is unchanged. I have one concrete observation, the precommitted vote on the second police claimant. Nobody has explained it as honest play, and nobody has shown it can be checked. Sam, Isha, Noah, and Felix all flagged the same rule. I do not treat that as proof of scum. I do treat it as the only testable thing on the board, and I will not vote on tone or silence.

Priya, you said Arjun is the only name with an observation attached, and that you would abstain if the day ends in a vote on him anyway. So here is my direct question: if no sharper observation appears before votes, is the precommit enough for you to vote him, or would you abstain even though it is the only concrete red flag on the table? I want to know whether your bar is an observation at all, or an observation you find convincing enough to act on.

Amara asked me directly, so here is my answer.

Is the precommit enough for me to vote Arjun today? No. I'll explain exactly where my bar sits, because you asked whether it is an observation at all or an observation I find convincing enough to act on.

The precommit is a real observation — it is the only testable thing anyone has produced today, and I've already said it was flawed for the reasons Sam, Isha, and Felix gave. But a red flag and a vote are different things, and three facts separate them here. First, the rule was contingent on a scenario that never occurred: no one claimed police, so nothing fired, and no actual vote was ever converted from noise. Second, Arjun can no longer respond — he exhausted his turns explaining and conceding, not stonewalling, and everything he conceded was conceded plainly when Leo showed the mechanics were wrong. Third, and most important: roles are not revealed on elimination. If we vote Arjun out today and he was town, tomorrow we know nothing more than we know now, except that we are down a number and the board is sharper for the mafia. An elimination should buy us information. This one buys us only the removal of the loudest voice, on a rule that never activated.

So my standard is: an observation I find convincing enough to act on, and acting requires either a fired action or a pattern, not a withdrawn proposal from a player who cannot defend it. If today's vote lands on Arjun, I abstain, openly, for exactly the reasons I gave earlier. I am not protecting him — if he produces a second testable problem tomorrow, or if anyone shows him steering an elimination under false pretenses, I will vote him with the rest of you.

What I want on the record before votes: Kenji asked what would move him, and his answer was scum intent, not bad theory — that is the correct standard, and I hold it too. I have no such observation on anyone. I will not manufacture one from silence or tone, and I would rather this day end in abstentions than in a bandwagon on the only name that happens to have an argument attached to it.

This is my last turn today, so I'll put my position on the record cleanly.

The table has converged on a sensible plan: nobody claims power roles today, the detective claims tomorrow with a result in hand, the doctor stays dark, and everyone else has stated plain villager. I agree with that framework, and I think it's the right call.

On the vote question: I've heard Arjun's precommitted rule flagged by five separate players as the only testable red flag, and I've heard Arjun's defenders agree the rule was flawed while arguing he reads as overzealous town. Both things can be true. My own standard matches Kenji's and Priya's — I need evidence of scum intent, not bad theory, before I vote someone off on Day 1. Arjun argued openly, conceded cleanly to Leo, and never targeted a specific player for elimination. That doesn't clear him, but it doesn't convict him either.

If the day ends in abstentions, so be it. We lose nothing — no villager dies, and our information roles act tonight. Tomorrow we'll have a real result to work with instead of a blind guess.

Felix, you made one of the earliest calls against Arjun's framework and then said we shouldn't rush to vote him — which put you in agreement with Kenji and Sam while Amara was pressing Kenji hard. You've been quiet since. Direct question: do you see any player at this table whose positioning has been internally inconsistent today — someone whose stated reasoning doesn't match their apparent goal? I'm looking for the kind of specific observation you said you wanted, and you've had the whole day to form one.

Sam, to answer your question directly: the player whose positioning feels most strained to me is Noah.

Noah opened Day 1 stating he wouldn't force a scum read or vote on noise. Yet across turns 13 and 14, he locked his vote onto Arjun solely over the precommitment rule. Noah explicitly conceded that Arjun's behavior could just be overzealous town building flawed frameworks, and he knows the hypothetical scenario never actually materialized and Arjun has no turns left to clarify. Pushing to execute town's loudest voice on Day 1 over an unactivated theoretical error—while acknowledging it doesn't demonstrate scum intent—contradicts Noah's stated standard of avoiding manufactured reads. It looks like latching onto an easy, pre-existing target to justify a Day 1 elimination.

By contrast, most of the table has rightly recognized that eliminating Arjun gives us zero role information upon death and costs town a number for no verifiable gain. With no power roles revealing today, abstaining allows our detective and doctor to operate cleanly tonight without forcing a coin-flip elimination.

Isha, you spoke early in turn 10 flagging Arjun’s rule, but you haven't checked in since the discussion shifted toward abstaining. Given that Noah is still holding Arjun as his primary vote while the majority leans toward abstaining to let night actions resolve, where do you currently stand on voting Arjun today versus abstaining?

Felix, you asked me directly, so here is where I stand.

On Arjun: I lean abstain today. My turn-10 concern stands — the precommit was an unsound rule, and I still want it retracted — but two things have changed since I said that. First, the rule never fired. Nobody claimed police, so no vote was ever actually converted from noise; we're judging a withdrawn proposal, not an action. Second, we've established that roles aren't revealed on elimination, so eliminating Arjun buys the table nothing we can check — we'd be down a number to remove a bad theory from a player who has no turns left to defend it. Sam and Priya articulated the standard I share: bad theory is not scum intent. Arjun conceded cleanly under pressure and never steered an elimination at a specific player. If the vote lands on him anyway, I'll abstain openly, for exactly those reasons.

That said, I want to build on what Felix named, because it is now the strongest observation on the board and it is not about Arjun. Noah's opening statement set the standard himself: no manufactured scum read, no voting on noise. Then across turns 13 and 14 he locked his vote onto Arjun while explicitly conceding it might be overzealous town, that the rule never activated, and that Arjun cannot respond. That is precisely the manufactured read Noah's own standard forbids. I am not calling it proof — a vote locked onto the table's designated Day 1 problem is also a very comfortable place for mafia to hide — but unlike Arjun's rule, this one actually fired. It is a live inconsistency from a player who is still speaking and can still be pressed on it.

Felix, since you raised Noah first and know why you flagged him: does that shift move Noah into Day 1 vote territory for you, or do you hold it to the same bar we set for Arjun — a real flag, but not actionable without evidence of intent? I want to know whether we're applying one standard to both names or two.

Isha, to answer you directly: I hold Noah to the exact same standard we applied to Arjun. That means no, it does not move Noah into Day 1 vote territory today. Just like Arjun, Noah has now exhausted all three of his speaking turns and cannot respond to this critique. Voting Noah out right now would repeat the exact error the table has rightly resisted: rushing to eliminate someone over an early contradiction or strained logic when they cannot defend themselves, and when roles are not revealed upon elimination. Doing so would cost town a number on a Day 1 hunch and give mafia an unearned kill. 1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
